clue.text: Estimable, like Hector and eight others

definitions.meaning: deserving respect and esteem, of real merit
the Nine Worthies were heroes of medieval legend, among them Hector of Troy, Alexander and Julius Caesar

explanation.walkthrough: The Nine Worthies were a medieval list of exemplary heroes: three pagan, three Jewish, three Christian; Hector is one of the pagan three.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: a person of merit is estimable, and Hector was one of the medieval Nine Worthies, so each of the nine was one.

clue.text: Is a fat man unpopular if given this on a cruise ?

definitions.text: Is a fat man unpopular if given this on a cruise ?

parts.words: Is a fat man unpopular if given this on a cruise ?
parts.note: a stout passenger needs a roomy bunk aboard ship, while giving someone plenty of room is how you avoid a person you dislike

explanation.surface: A question about whether a portly passenger is snubbed on a cruise ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the two senses: the large man gets a broad bunk for his size, yet the idiom suggests people are keeping clear of him.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a broad sleeping bunk on a ship, and also, idiomatically, the room you leave when steering clear of someone.

clue.text: They used to press charges

parts.note: reads like accusers in court, but the charges are loads of powder and shot rammed down the barrel of an old muzzle-loading gun

explanation.surface: People who once brought legal accusations against others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'press charges' is the legal phrase for accusing someone; here the charges are gunpowder loads, and 'used to' fits because muzzle-loaders are long obsolete.
explanation.definitionFit: These rods were used to push the powder and ball down the barrel of a muzzle-loading firearm.

clue.text: Menial manicurist

definitions.meaning: a female servant or attendant, someone doing humble work
read as a young woman who looks after hands

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is cryptic: take the word apart as HAND and MAIDEN to see a woman who works on hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: a female servant is a menial, and split into two words it suggests a girl who tends hands, as a manicurist does.

clue.text: Do they try to live up to their name ?

definitions.text: Do they try to live up to their name ?

parts.words: Do they try to live up to their name ?
parts.note: people who test or taste things try them out, so their very name describes that trying; the word also names embroidered cloths

explanation.surface: A musing on whether people strive to deserve the label they carry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'try' is taken in the sense of testing: a taster tries things, so in trying they do just what their name says.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who try things out by tasting or testing them are the people the word names, which is also a term for embroidered needlework pieces.

clue.text: Powerful motor barons?

parts.note: an absolute ruler is a powerful baron of sorts, and the first syllables also suggest car, as in automobile

explanation.surface: Mighty tycoons of the car industry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'motor' points to the AUTO at the start of the word, as in automobile, though the word really means rulers who govern alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Absolute rulers wield unchecked power, and the word begins with the prefix that means car, so it suggests car-making magnates.

clue.text: Not a driver's favourite colour

parts.note: a pale red shade, but also the knocking sound a car engine makes when fuel ignites too early, which no motorist wants to hear

explanation.surface: A remark on which paint shade motorists dislike.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English an engine 'pinks' (US: 'pings' or knocks) when the fuel detonates too early, so the colour is one no driver wants to hear.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a pale red shade, and as a verb it describes the metallic knock of a badly firing engine, a fault drivers dread.

clue.text: Now here is a novel reform

indicators.note: to reform is to form again, so these letters are made into a new shape

explanation.surface: A claim that a book about social change has just arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform' looks like social change but it is the anagram signal: NOW HERE rearranged gives the title of Butler's novel, which itself plays on the word 'nowhere'.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Butler's 1872 satire is named after an imaginary land, and its title is a near-reversal of the place it stands for.

clue.text: A meaningful faculty

parts.note: one of the bodily faculties such as sight or hearing, and also a word for meaning, so it is a faculty that is full of meaning

explanation.surface: A university department that has real significance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'faculty' suggests a university department, but it is a natural power such as sight; 'meaningful' points to the word's other sense, meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Sight, hearing and touch are each one of these faculties, and the same word means the meaning of a phrase.

clue.text: It's a trial, and indeed intensely disliked

indicators.note: the clue's 'indeed' is read as 'in deed': the answer sits within the word deed

parts.note: hated, loathed
an act or action, taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that something is an ordeal and thoroughly hated.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'indeed' as 'in DEED': putting the answer inside DEED makes DETESTED, the word for 'intensely disliked', so taking DEED out of DETESTED leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An exam or experiment is a trial of ability or quality.

clue.text: I do mine wrong for teacher

indicators.note: the letters are put together wrongly, i.e. in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Someone admitting they work a mine badly.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of I DO MINE gives a Scottish word for a schoolmaster, best known from Walter Scott's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Scots word for a schoolmaster, used for a village schoolteacher.

clue.text: The abbey front, at any rate, is colourful

definitions.text: The abbey front, at any rate, is colourful

parts.words: The abbey front, at any rate, is colourful
parts.note: names a ruined Welsh abbey whose first four letters spell a word for a shade or hue

explanation.surface: A remark that an abbey's facade, at least, is brightly painted.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'front' is the start of the word: its opening letters spell TINT, a colour, so the front of this abbey is colourful. The abbey is a ruined monastery in the Wye valley in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The ruined Cistercian monastery in the Wye valley, made famous by Wordsworth, begins with a word for a shade of colour.

clue.text: Made of witch-hazel ?

parts.note: witch-hazel is a shrub, but read as a witch's hazel wood it suggests the handle of the besom a witch rides

explanation.surface: A question about what material something is made from: a medicinal shrub.
explanation.walkthrough: Witch-hazel is a real shrub used in lotions; split it as 'witch hazel' and it becomes a witch's piece of hazel wood, the handle she flies on.
explanation.definitionFit: A witch's traditional means of flight is a besom with a wooden handle, which could be cut from hazel.

clue.text: The beginning and the end of the second person

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only the final letter of the third word 'the' is taken; the letters running across 'the end' are a coincidence, not a hidden word

explanation.surface: A grammar note: how the word 'the' opens and closes a second-person form.
explanation.walkthrough: THE is the beginning, and the end of the word 'the' is E, giving the old second-person pronoun used in the Bible and in prayers.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic object pronoun for 'you', addressing one person directly, as in prayers.

clue.text: It's just lost by a second

definitions.text: It's just lost by a second

parts.words: It's just lost by a second
parts.note: sounds like a narrow time margin, but the runner-up, who comes second, loses out on the top award

explanation.surface: A race decided by a single second on the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a second' looks like a unit of time; it is the person who comes second, who by definition just misses the top award.
explanation.definitionFit: The top award goes to the winner, so the competitor who comes second misses it, often narrowly.

clue.text: Nationality of sweet Charlotte ?

parts.note: Charlotte russe is a dessert of sponge fingers and cream, so this sweet is from Moscow's country by its name

explanation.surface: A question about where a lovely girl named Charlotte comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweet Charlotte' seems to be a charming woman; it is the pudding charlotte russe, whose French name means the Russian charlotte.
explanation.definitionFit: The cold dessert charlotte russe takes its name from the French word for someone from Russia's country.

clue.text: A yearning that proved fatal to Mrs Lot

definitions.text: A yearning that proved fatal to Mrs Lot

parts.words: A yearning that proved fatal to Mrs Lot
parts.note: in Genesis, Lot's wife looked back at Sodom and was turned into a pillar of salt; a longing for the past is a looking back

explanation.surface: A biblical woman whose longing led to her death.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis, Lot's wife disobeyed and looked back at the burning city, and was turned into a pillar of salt; the answer is a longing to look back.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a wistful longing for the past, a backward look of the heart, like the glance that turned Lot's wife to salt.

clue.text: Crooked dealing made straight

indicators.note: crooked means bent out of shape, so the letters of the following word are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: Dishonest business practices have been put right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crooked dealing' reads as fraud, but 'Crooked' is the anagram signal for DEALING; the contrast with 'straight' is the clue's point.
explanation.definitionFit: Things set in a straight line, or brought into line, have been straightened.

clue.text: By no means a constructive addition to naval power

definitions.text: By no means a constructive addition to naval power

parts.words: By no means a constructive addition to naval power
parts.note: a fast warship adds to a navy, but its name says it wrecks rather than builds

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict that a new acquisition does nothing to help the navy.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on the warship's name: it does add to naval power, but literally it is one who wrecks, not one who builds.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast escort warship strengthens a fleet, yet its name means a wrecker, the opposite of constructive.

clue.text: Chaps are so unlucky if they lose heart

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letters, here the word with its first and last letters removed

parts.note: losing something leaves you with less of it, so the word gives less

explanation.surface: Men are unfortunate if they become discouraged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lose heart' looks like an idiom for despair. Take the heart of CHAPS (HAP, without its first and last letters) and add LESS for 'lose'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ill-starred and luckless has no good fortune at all.

clue.text: Though written under, it need not be used by underwriters

definitions.text: Though written under, it need not be used by underwriters

parts.words: Though written under, it need not be used by underwriters
parts.note: authors write under an assumed name, but insurance underwriters sign their own

explanation.surface: A remark about insurance signatories and the names they sign.
explanation.walkthrough: One writes 'under' a pseudonym, which suggests underwriters, the insurers who sign policies; they have no need of a false name.
explanation.definitionFit: Authors who wish to stay anonymous publish under an invented name, so their work is written under it.

clue.text: Chekhovian trio

parts.note: Chekhov's play about Olga, Masha and Irina, three siblings longing for Moscow

explanation.surface: A group of three from a Russian playwright's work.
explanation.walkthrough: The play is 'Three Sisters'; the trio are its three heroines.
explanation.definitionFit: Chekhov's 1901 play follows Olga, Masha and Irina, three female siblings stuck in a provincial town.

clue.text: Reveal the route of Lots escape

definitions.meaning: make clear, set out, account for
Lot fled from Sodom, one of the cities of the plain, so his route was out of the plain

explanation.walkthrough: Read the word as EX PLAIN, 'out of the plain': in Genesis, Lot escaped from Sodom and Gomorrah, the cities of the plain.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: to make something clear is to reveal it, and Lot left the cities of the plain, an exit from the plain.

clue.text: These containers would be of service to Mother

definitions.text: would be of service to Mother
definitions.meaning: put after MA, a word for mother, they would make MATINS, the morning church service

explanation.walkthrough: MA (mother) followed by these letters gives MATINS, the morning church service.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: metal cans are containers, and added to MA they make the morning service, so they serve Mother.

clue.text: Trunk with twisted roots

indicators.note: twisted means turned out of shape, so the letters of the following word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tree with gnarled roots.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a tree, but 'Trunk' is the body's middle, and 'twisted' rearranges ROOTS.
explanation.definitionFit: The human body without head and limbs is called the trunk, like the main stem of a tree.

clue.text: Appears wet-anyway, put it in the basket

indicators.note: anyhow, in any old way, so the letters are put together in any order

explanation.surface: Something that seems soaked, so just bin it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' signals that APPEARS WET is rearranged; soggy paper is what you would throw away, so the surface fits the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Discarded sheets and scraps belong in the rubbish bin beside the desk.

clue.text: Bath's visitors use them off and on

definitions.text: Bath's visitors use them off and on

parts.words: Bath's visitors use them off and on
parts.note: Bath is a spa city, but read as a bathtub, its fittings are turned off and on

explanation.surface: Tourists in the spa city of Bath come and go now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is an English spa city visited by tourists; read as a bathtub, its users turn these fittings off and on.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathtub fittings let water flow and stop, turned on and off by the bather.

clue.text: Spoony companion in an elopement

parts.note: in the nursery rhyme 'Hey Diddle Diddle', a piece of crockery ran away with the spoon

explanation.surface: A lovesick partner running off to marry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoony' seems to mean lovesick, but it means of the spoon: in the rhyme 'the dish ran away with the spoon'.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'Hey Diddle Diddle' a plate ran away with the spoon, so it was the spoon's partner in eloping.

clue.text: University of books

parts.note: names an English town with a university, and also the act of perusing books

explanation.surface: An academic institution devoted to books.
explanation.walkthrough: The University of Reading is in the town of that name in Berkshire, west of London; 'of books' gives the other sense, perusing them.
explanation.definitionFit: There is a university in this Berkshire town, and the word also means perusing books.

clue.text: First-class education ?

parts.note: first-class suggests the best schooling, but it is the first stage of school, for young children

explanation.surface: Asking about a top-quality schooling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First-class' seems to mean excellent; it means the first classes in school, the early-years stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The earliest stage of schooling, for young children, comes first in the sequence.

clue.text: Such charges would not include ground-rent 'presumably

definitions.text: Such charges would not include ground-rent 'presumably

parts.words: Such charges would not include ground-rent 'presumably
parts.note: running costs of a business are charges taken literally as being up in the air, so not rent for the ground

explanation.surface: A note on which costs exclude rent for land.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken literally, the word for running costs means 'above the head', so it could not include rent for the ground beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A business's running costs, such as heating and rent, are its fixed expenses, which the word suggests are up above.

clue.text: Of more appeal to Jack than to Mrs. Sprat

definitions.text: Of more appeal to Jack than to Mrs. Sprat

parts.words: Of more appeal to Jack than to Mrs. Sprat
parts.note: in the nursery rhyme Jack Sprat could eat no fat and his wife could eat no lean meat

explanation.surface: A comparison of what a husband and wife like.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme, Jack Sprat ate only lean meat and his wife only fat, so meat with less fat appeals more to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat with less fat on it suited Jack Sprat, who 'could eat no fat', while his wife 'could eat no lean'.
